articles.title: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, sobre su cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez: “Le pusimos ante el espejo de su corrupción y mala gestión y ofrecimos una España mejor”
articles.standfirst: El líder del PP se pronunció en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife
articles.summary: El líder del PP se pronunció en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife
articles.body: En poco más de una semana tendrán lugar las elecciones generales a la presidencia del Gobierno en nuestro país. El domingo, 29 de noviembre (29N) los españoles acudirán a las urnas en una jornada que acaparará todas las miradas. En este contexto, los diferentes líderes de los partidos políticos nacionales siguen con sus mítines y entrevistas a lo largo de toda la geografía española. En este contexto, en la noche de este jueves, 19 de noviembre, se dio uno de los momentos más esperados de cara a esta cita. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, líder del PP, y Pedro Sánchez, del PSOE y actual jefe del Ejecutivo, se dieron cita para el segundo debate electoral entre ambos desde el que tuvo lugar en 2023. El dirigente popular, según apuntan los expertos en materia política, salió mejor parado que el actual presidente del Gobierno. Pues bien, el propio mandatario de la formación azul se pronunció sobre este cara a cara en un mitin celebrado en Tenerife. Feijóo comenzó pronunciándose así al respecto: “Solo hice lo mismo que llevo haciendo los últimos tres años de esta legislatura. Un relato de los hechos y de lo que ha sufrido España durante este tiempo. Ofrecí la alternativa que llevo construyendo cuatro años para que nuestro país funcione”. Del mismo modo, el líder de la oposición recalcó que se debatió con las “mismas” reglas, el “mismo” tiempo y “sin “intermediarios”: "Pudimos hablar cara a cara y los españoles vieron una realidad”, añadió. “No es el relato que le interesa a Sánchez. Ayer pusimos a Sánchez ante el espejo de su corrupción, de su mala gestión y ofrecimos una España mejor”, sentenció Alberto Núñez Feijóo ante los aplausos de todos los presentes en el evento celebrado en Tenerife.

articles.title: Trump responds after Vance blames Iran war for midterm losses, VP says his job is to support president
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says he would launch the war against Iran again, as JD Vance blames midterm losses on voter anger over the conflict and oil prices.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Friday that he would still have launched the military operation against Iran, pushing back against reports of friction with Vice President JD Vance after Vance attributed Republican midterm election losses to the ongoing conflict. Speaking to reporters following his trip to Asia, Trump addressed questions about whether he was displeased with Vance’s post-election assessment that the conflict drove Democratic gains in the next Congress. "I didn't say I was unhappy with it," Trump said alongside Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that if we're asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ Absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon." VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' The remarks followed a series of posts on X by Vance a day after the midterm elections, in which Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate — along with the Texas governorship — blaming voter frustration over the conflict and elevated oil prices. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY On Friday, Trump called Vance's assessment "accurate" and acknowledged that fuel costs rose amid the fighting, though he said the spike was milder than anticipated. "The war drove up prices, fuel prices far less than I thought," Trump said. "I thought it would go up to $300 a barrel. You know, it's almost down to $80 a barrel right now." FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS Despite the political fallout, Trump maintained that the military action was necessary to counter Tehran’s nuclear ambitions and to protect Israel and other Middle Eastern nations. Vance affirmed that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon justified the political cost, while emphasizing his alignment with Trump. RUBIO DEFENDS TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS NOT 'NECESSARILY POPULAR, BUT NECESSARY' "What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing," Vance said. "It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially, of innocent people." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance added. "My view is that my goal, and my job, is to support the president of the United States."

articles.title: Somali community leaders bristle at broad blame even as youth gang violence surges from Minnesota to Maine
articles.summary: Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher says about 100 of 300 young alleged Somali gang members in the Twin Cities were arrested, but many cycle back into gang life.
articles.body: Somali community members in Minnesota pushed back Thursday against blaming the broader Somali American population as law enforcement officials warned of a surge in youth gang violence. Members of the Somali community and law enforcement leaders met to discuss gang-related crimes in the Twin Cities, KSTP 5 Eyewitness News reported Thursday. Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher estimates there are about a dozen Somali gangs involving roughly 300 young people in the metro area out of an estimated 1,000 to 2,000 total gang members across the region. Fletcher said many gang members who do get arrested ultimately continue participating in "the gang life." CULTURE CLASH LAID BARE AS VIOLENT SOMALI GANGS GRIP SUBURBAN COMMUNITIES: ‘THESE KIDS ARE DIFFERENT’ "Well, many of them are [arrested]. articles.title: Musk said he'd "look into" this disclosure law. Now it heads to court.
articles.summary: Two county prosecutors say the Trump administration broke the law when it exempted U.S. companies from ownership reporting.
articles.body:
In March 2025, a conservative comedian named Terrence K. Williams had a plea for Elon Musk: ask President Trump to scrap a " ridiculous " federal rule that forced companies to disclose their true owners.

"I'm begging you!" Williams posted on X, Musk's social media platform. "It's targeting conservatives and small businesses!"

The billionaire replied , "I can look into it."

A day later, the Trump administration took action. In a post on X , the Treasury Department announced it would no longer enforce penalties or fines against U.S. citizens, domestic companies or their owners under the law, known as the Corporate Transparency Act.

Now, two local prosecutors are suing to stop the administration from erasing roughly 15 million company ownership records it has already collected, CBS News has learned.

On Thursday, the top prosecutors in Hennepin County, Minnesota, and Pima County, Arizona — Mary Moriarty and Laura Conover — alleged in a lawsuit that the Treasury Department violated the law when it exempted American companies from the disclosure rules and let foreign companies leave out their American owners.

Moriarty and Conover, both Democrats, say the ownership records would help their offices pursue cartel money laundering, wage theft, fraud and organized retail theft carried out through shell companies. The suit also names Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose departments had to sign off on the exemptions.

Deleting the records would make it "easier than ever for criminals to use shell and front companies for illicit activities and evade detection," the lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., says. It argues that "because law enforcement cannot know in advance which companies will warrant scrutiny, the value of beneficial-ownership reporting lies in collecting that information before the need for it arises."

In a statement to CBS News, a Treasury spokesperson said removing the reporting requirement was "a victory for common sense," adding that the department made the change "after careful consideration of the costs to small business owners and the benefit to national security."

The agency did not respond to questions about whether Musk reached out to Treasury about the rule. A spokesperson for Musk did not respond to requests for comment.

The lawsuit escalates a fight between Democrats and the Trump administration over the rollback, which critics have scrutinized for its timing. The complaint cites Musk's exchange with Williams, saying he had "set his sights on" the disclosure rule while leading the Department of Government Efficiency. Democrats in Congress have questioned Musk's possible role since April 2025, when they wrote to the Treasury Department that the decision was "seemingly triggered by a single Elon Musk social media comment."

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, along with California Rep. Maxine Waters, said in a March 2026 letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Musk "uses a network of dozens of secretive companies" that could potentially be required to share ownership information under the law.

"This rule started with an Elon Musk post on X and will end with 15 million documents in the shredder," said Brendan Ballou, a former Justice Department prosecutor whose firm, the Public Integrity Project, is representing the plaintiffs.

The Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security declined to comment.

The Corporate Transparency Act became law in January 2021 with bipartisan support, after Congress included it in a defense bill and overrode Mr. Trump's veto of the broader package. Then-Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, one of its champions and now Mr. Trump's secretary of state, called it in 2020 "the most significant anti-corruption [and] money laundering law in decades."

The law's aim was to combat money laundering and illicit finance by requiring companies to report their true owners to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a Treasury Department office known as FinCEN. The reporting requirement took effect in 2024, covering nearly 33 million companies , until the Trump administration narrowed it to foreign firms.

By then, U.S. companies had filed about 15 million reports with FinCEN, according to the Treasury Department.

In August 2026, the agency said it plans to delete them in "one sweep of the database" and will notify the public on its website once it's done.

Supporters of the law say it helps investigators follow the money behind crimes like sanctions evasion, drug trafficking and smuggling.

"The only way that you can actually create an easy chain to examine these flows is if you're able to unmask who's behind all these types of transactions," said Max Meizlish, a former career Treasury sanctions official who is now a fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a foreign policy think tank.

In its final rule, the Treasury Department argued the requirement placed "costs of time and money" on "law-abiding American small businesses," and said the rollback would save billions of dollars a year. The department concluded that requiring domestic companies to report their owners "would not serve the public interest," and that "indiscriminate collection" of that information "would not provide law enforcement with highly valuable information."

A number of Republicans have long said that the law buried mom-and-pop companies in paperwork and threatened them with steep financial penalties . In January 2025, Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville and Ohio Rep. Warren Davidson reintroduced a bill to repeal the law entirely. Tuberville called it "big-government overreach at its worst."

Not all Republicans welcomed the rollback, though. Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, who co-sponsored an earlier version of the law with Whitehouse, urged Treasury in 2025 to scrap its initial rollback. When the final rule came out in August 2026, the two senators said in a joint statement that it "undermines the clear intent of the law."

Without the corporate records, the lawsuit argues, investigators must subpoena bank after bank to learn who is behind a shell company, a slow process that often yields thin or inaccurate answers. The prosecutors are asking a judge to throw out the rule and stop the deletion.

"Wage thieves and fraudsters hide behind shell companies because it works," Moriarty said in a statement. "The only people who benefit are the ones we are trying to catch."

articles.title: Trump wags finger at 'really rude' reporter, tells her she belongs in the 'back row' during press exchange
articles.summary: Donald Trump wagged his finger at a reporter, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row" at the White House.
articles.body: President Donald Trump rebuked a female reporter at the end of a White House news conference Friday, wagging his finger at her, calling her "really a rude person" and telling her she belonged in the "back row." The exchange unfolded as Trump wrapped up a lengthy news conference following his return from an Asia trip, just after inviting White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller to the podium and praising Miller's work on immigration and deregulation. Before addressing the press corps, Trump defended Miller's temperament, noting that critics often view him as overly strict on immigration. But we’ll talk about that," Trump said before breaking off to address the journalist. "Who are you with. Who are you with?" Trump asked while waving his finger in her direction. After the reporter replied, "Who are you?" Trump sharply criticized both her demeanor and her seating placement in the room. JOE ROGAN SAYS PODCASTERS HAVE NO BUSINESS AT TRUMP PRESS CONFERENCES ALONGSIDE REAL JOURNALISTS "And you’re really a rude person," Trump said. articles.title: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
articles.summary: Donald Trump stunned the White House press briefing room by asking Stephen Miller if he wants to run for president, as JD Vance and Marco Rubio looked on.
articles.body: During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by. The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing. Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press. MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028 Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office. "I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said. He then rattled some of them off, including: "Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader." Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans. "We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference. "Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group. STEPHEN MILLER'S INTERNAL MEMO UNLEASHES TRUMP AGENCIES AFTER 'ABSOLUTE CONTROL' UNDER WILES' REIGN No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028. But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring. Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans. articles.title: Hinojosa outlines plans to end family detention at controversial ICE facility
articles.summary: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) shared her plan this week to end family detention at a controversial immigration detention center in the state in a conversation with YouTube children’s creator Ms. Rachel. “The reason we believe the children are being detained here with their families is because there’s licensing that allows that to happen,” Hinojosa…
articles.body:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) shared her plan this week to end family detention at a controversial immigration detention center in the state in a conversation with YouTube children’s creator Ms. Rachel.

“The reason we believe the children are being detained here with their families is because there’s licensing that allows that to happen,” Hinojosa said in a video shared Thursday on Instagram. “I would not allow that to happen. I would not ever license that — that’s child abuse. Should not be happening.”

The YouTube star, whose full name is Rachel Accurso, has taken a public stand to advocate against Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) practice of detaining families at Texas’s Dilley Immigration Processing Center.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Earlier this month, Hinojosa told The New York Times she planned to use the state’s licensing power to prevent private prison companies from holding children in detention facilities in the state. Dilley is run by the private prison operator CoreCivic under contract with ICE.

“Locking up little kids like that, even with their parents, that is child abuse,” Hinojosa told the outlet.

Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) responded to the Times article, saying he looked forward to working with Hinojosa to “shut down the Dilley Trailer Prison once and for all.”

“We must end family detention in America,” he wrote on social media . “No child should be ripped away from their lives and locked away. No private company should profit from the suffering and trauma of children.”

Castro visited the immigration processing center in January to meet with five-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos and his father, Adrian Conejo Arias, after they were detained and transported to the facility following their arrests in Minnesota.

The Democratic representative announced the pair’s release and return to Minnesota on Feb. 1, and he has continued to advocate for the end of family detention practices.

Hinojosa told Accurso that she was open to working with President Trump to “take care of kids and families.”

“Because we should be able to come together to stop hurting kids in this country and in this state,” she added.

During a press conference on Friday, President Trump said he recently spoke with Hinojosa and that she was “really nice.”

“It was a very productive call, and she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out,” he said. “Because that’s a very important thing. I got elected on the border, I did a phenomenal job.”

articles.title: The GOP’s 2028 hopefuls navigate their party’s midterm wipeout: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Kristen Welker dives into the early jockeying among the class of Republican White House contenders. Plus, Gary Grumbach explores why the Trump administration is moving on from its frequent voter fraud claims. — Adam Wollner The GOP’s 2028 hopefuls navigate their party’s midterm wipeout Analysis by Kristen Welker The dust has barely settled from the midterms, but there’s already been a lot of movement from potential Democratic presidential contenders ahead of what’s expected to be a sprawling contest reminiscent of the 20-plus person field from 2020. While the positioning on the Republican side has so far been more subtle, it’s been equally notable. In the weeks since the GOP suffered massive election losses, Vice President JD Vance has been trying to re-emphasize the “America” in “Make America Great Again.” He’s distancing himself from the Iran war, sparring with a Republican governor on social media over immigration, and using a Fox News interview to invoke his call for “economic nationalism” and to “reindustrialize in the United States.” Vance is not the only one emphasizing economic populism as the path forward for the bruised Republican Party. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., went from saying he has “no intention” of running for president in 2028 just two months ago to telling NBC News’ Allan Smith yesterday that he’s giving “serious thought” to what his political future might entail, not ruling out a White House bid. Like Vance, Hawley emphasized how voters want to “get focused back on us, back on the blue-collar family that’s just trying to make it.” But unlike Vance, Hawley’s comments that “I’m not really a supporter of” the war with Iran are cleaner given his perch from outside the administration. Even if the election results have diminished Trump’s political sway, he is still the primary force in Republican politics right now. And that’s why I’m paying close attention to how he talks about the race to be his successor. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio flanked Trump in the White House briefing room today as he held a news conference after returning from his trip to China. In an interview yesterday with NBC News’ Gabe Gutierrez, Trump said of Vance and Rubio, “They’re both doing a great job.” The topic of the Iran war came up again during the press briefing. Asked if the war was worth Republicans losing control of the Senate, Vance responded: “I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.” And earlier, Trump was asked about Vance’s post-election social media post saying that the Iran war is the reason for the GOP’s losses. Trump said, “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said — would you do it again? And absolutely. The answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” Outside of Washington, some of the tech billionaires who cozied up to Trump after he took office last year are now seeking some distance from the MAGA brand after the midterms. That includes Elon Musk, who gave hundreds of millions of dollars to help Republicans this election cycle and previously served as a Trump White House adviser. Trump told Gabe yesterday, “MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well.” While it was technically in response to Musk, it’s a comment that could serve as a warning to those who believe their path to the presidency is by breaking from Trump’s vision for the GOP. It’s against this backdrop that I’m looking forward to speaking with Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who told me last month that he’s weighing his own presidential bid, on “Meet the Press” this Sunday. And as Senate Democrats chart their path forward with their large new majority, I’ll also interview Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to be the leader of the chamber, and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich. I hope you’ll join me. DOJ’s focus on voter fraud fades post-midterms By Gary Grumbach Democrats flew election lawyers to key battleground states. Republicans recruited tens of thousands of volunteer poll watchers from coast to coast. The Justice Department implemented its largest election monitoring operation ever, after ramping up investigations of possible noncitizen voting. Department of Homeland Security officials threatened to hold up federal funding unless states complied with new election security measures. But in the end, most of those resources weren’t needed. The 2026 midterm elections largely went off without a hitch. It’s a stark departure from the doomsday election scenario that President Donald Trump and top members of his administration warned Americans about for nearly two years, as they raised fears of widespread noncitizen voting, including suggestions that Democrats might seek to rig the midterms. But following Democrats’ decisive victory, the DOJ is dropping its appeals involving its litigation against states over potential voting concerns. Yesterday, the DOJ asked an appeals court to toss a civil suit it filed last month in Alaska that sought to block certification of the Senate election if GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan lost. “Elections officials and civil society were as prepared as I’ve ever seen them, in 25 years of election work, to make sure that the process would be resistant and resilient to attempted disruption — and that preparation paid off,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Marymount University who served as a White House policy adviser for democracy and voting under the Biden administration. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

Trump shakes up cybersecurity leadership

The White House capped off a dramatic week of tech outages with a high-profile departure in its cybersecurity leadership.

Sean Cairncross , the national cyber director, was let go from the role this week — the latest in a number of recent White House leadership shakeups.

President Trump backed the decision to let go of Cairncross because he didn’t think he had the cyber credentials for the job, a White House official told The Hill Thursday night.

The decision followed days of confusion and scrutiny about a wave of system outages that hit various sectors, including banks, tech companies and aviation.

The Trump administration faced pressure to explain the reason behind these outages and, in the wake of such answers, conspiracy theories about cyberattacks and a so-called AI “doomsday” flooded the internet.

It’s not clear whether the White House’s response was what led to Carincross’s departure, but online users were quick to speculate on the timing.

Cairncross sat at the top of the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), which manages cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. He previously served as chief of staff on National Security Council committees during Trump’s first term and then as an executive for the Millennium Challenge Corporation from 2019 to 2021.

Kirsten Davies , the Pentagon’s chief information officer, is assuming the role in an acting capacity. The White House believes she has the credentials for the position, the official said.

While ONCD has often managed to keep a lower profile in past presidencies, the advancements of AI have propelled cybersecurity concerns to the forefront over the past year as the tool becomes a potential weapon for adversaries and hackers.

The now-former ONCD director reportedly clashed with other leaders of the president’s Cabinet on these issues.

He allegedly believed the Treasury Department had become too involved with the team’s efforts, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his allies argued Cairncross had not been urgent with responding to questions about AI, according to Axios, which first reported on the departure.

articles.body:
President Trump sought to regain momentum Friday with a White House news conference that lasted almost 90 minutes.

Trump’s ostensible purpose was to talk up the achievements from his recent trip to Asia, which included the announcement of trade deals and, more controversially, a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

On Friday, Trump was accompanied at the podium of the White House briefing room by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the presumptive front-runners for the GOP’s 2028 presidential nomination if they enter the race.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But there was much more news than that. Here are five takeaways.

Trump strikes defensive tone over midterms defeat

The news conference came against the backdrop of the GOP’s big defeat in the midterm elections, in which Democrats easily took control of the House and flipped nine Senate seats for a comfortable majority in the upper chamber.

The results were widely seen as a rebuke to Trump, whose poll ratings have been languishing near all-time lows.

On Friday, Trump seemed in a rather sour mood about it.

“I wasn’t on the ballot, I hope you remember that,” he told the press corps at one point. Moments later, he insisted, “If I were on the ballot, it would have been a whole different story.”

At one stage, he appeared to insinuate that the price of oil had been artificially kept elevated through the midterm elections to hurt his party’s chances.

It wasn’t clear whose hidden hand he felt was involved in this supposed sabotage. High gas prices have a far simpler explanation — the war on Iran, which Trump launched earlier this year.

While speaking about the midterms, Trump also claimed, “People thought that I was not treated well by the Republican Party because they didn’t get the things that I wanted passed.”

A fresh furor over Trump’s ‘friend’ Putin

One of the most controversial moments in Trump’s Asia trip came when he greeted Putin, saying, “He’s my friend.”

The president fueled the furor rather than tamping it down Friday.

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins asked Trump if he believed Putin to be a friend “to America.”

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump replied. “I’ve been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia-Russia-Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it.”

The first five words of that response, seeming to dismiss the national interest, were a bad soundbite, at best, for Trump. Beyond that, his desire to once again relitigate decade-old accusations of collusion between his 2016 campaign and Moscow has little salience to anyone outside of his MAGA base.

More broadly, Trump continues to characterize the war in Ukraine as driven by “serious animosity” between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. On Friday, he again seemed reluctant to focus on the actual cause of the war — Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Critics of Trump object more generally to his apparent admiration of authoritarian leaders. This was evident again at the press conference, beyond his comments on Putin, when he referred to Xi as “a great man” who had “done a fantastic job for the country.”

It fell to Rubio to make a more strategic argument for these expressions of warmth.

The secretary of State defended the trilateral meeting by saying that it would be “dangerous” if leaders like Trump, Xi and Putin were not able to engage with each other in a “conducive” environment.

One of the more interesting analyses of the midterms came from the vice president, when he wrote in a lengthy social media post right afterward that “the reason we lost is the war.”

This stark statement on the conflict in Iran was reported to have irked Trump, though the president has publicly denied annoyance.

Trump said Friday that Vance’s statement was “fine — except I would have had one other thing that people were asking. I would have said that, would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

But, he insisted, there was “no problem there at all” with what Vance had said.

The issue is playing out against the backdrop of two other factors: Vance’s presumed 2028 ambitions, and the belief that he was more reluctant to back an attack on Iran than any other senior member of the administration.

Vance hardly put the chatter to rest when he was asked at the news conference whether he personally felt the war was worth losing control of the Senate.

The vice president did not answer directly, instead citing the importance of keeping Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

He added: “The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again. … My job is to support the president of the United States.”

The side-stepping of the core question — what is Vance’s personal view? — was glaring.

Trump has seemed to go back and forth since the midterms on whether he is inclined to try to work with Democrats or whether he will double down on a confrontational approach.

On Friday, he seemed more inclined toward the first approach — slightly.

The president did, to be sure, emphasize the power of the presidential veto. He said he was willing to use it repeatedly if Democrats passed legislation that he deemed unacceptable.

However, Trump also suggested that this approach could ultimately pave the way to more constructive discussions between him and Democrats in Congress.

He highlighted healthcare as one potential area of common ground, as well as the possibility of trying to boost the TV and movie production industry and reforming college sports.

Of course, Trump could revert to antagonism at a moment’s notice. But his comments for now seem to at least keep the door ajar to bipartisan legislation.

Another 2028 audition — with a Stephen Miller cameo

The visual effect of Vance and Rubio standing behind Trump on the podium was guaranteed to bring more speculation about each man’s electoral strength for 2028.

Each offered eager support for Trump when they spoke. Rubio addressed the room for longer than Vance, in part to defend the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting. The vice president spoke more briefly about trade deals and boosts to industry.

But the wild card came when Stephen Miller, newly promoted to be White House chief of staff, was summoned to the lectern by Trump.

Miller is an enormously divisive figure, in part because of his hard-line approach to immigration and his extremely expansive view of presidential power.

Miller, speaking in his usual rapid-fire style, insisted that Trump had achieved more in the first two years of his second term than any other president “by far.” He further predicted that “the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history.”

This earned him a return in adulation from a happy president.

“He was better than these two guys,” Trump said, referring to Vance and Rubio. “Do you want to run for president?”

There is no realistic chance of Miller running to succeed Trump, but the admiring remark was a reminder of the chief of staff’s standing.

On the other hand, that had been clear even from the moment Trump introduced Miller on Friday.

“We have the most powerful man in the world in the room right now,” Trump said. “Chief of staff Stephen Miller.”

articles.body:
Senate Republican leaders convened a rare Friday session to vote on a slate of President Trump’s judicial nominees. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has said he wants to confirm as many judges, who will serve for life, as possible before Democrats take power in January.

“President Trump has more active judges on the appellate and district benches in this country than any other president,” Thune said in a floor speech earlier this week. “And that doesn’t happen by chance or happen by accident; it happens because we have been committed here in the United States Senate to ensuring that his judges move across the finish line at a fast pace.

After confirming two and teeing up final votes on five, the Senate left for Thanksgiving break.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), the Republican whip, said in a speech Tuesday that confirming Trump’s judicial nominees is “the top priority” of Senate Republicans for the lame-duck session and repeated that Republicans “will leave no vacancy behind.”

He also praised the qualifications of the nominees and the judges confirmed so far and criticized Democrats for refusing to provide consent for judges to be easily confirmed during this Congress, slowing down the process.

“Democrats want to paralyze President Trump and derail anyone who challenges their liberal ideology,” Barrasso said. “In the days and weeks ahead, Republicans will continue to burst through the Democrat blockade.”

Confirming nominees, including judges, is one of the Senate’s unique constitutional powers. But rules and procedures in the upper chamber also allow a single senator to hold up or block a judge nomination under some circumstances.

One judge won’t receive a vote anytime soon: T. Elliot Gaiser, Trump’s nominee for a district court in Texas, is currently awaiting a “blue slip,” or stamp of approval from outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). Cornyn is opposed to Gaiser because the latter is not from Texas and “has not been vetted.”

But generally, Republicans have supported Trump’s nominees.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), who is on the Judiciary Committee, said he was glad the Senate had put so much emphasis on judges this Congress. He added that the Senate has confirmed Trump-appointed judges for all the vacancies in Missouri, which he said is significant for providing a Republican majority among the district judges in the state.

“We want to get as many on the bench as possible,” Hawley said. “I imagine we won’t get much opportunity here soon.”

articles.body:
Collins, Shaheen push for insulin price cap

A bipartisan pair of departing New England senators is making a last-minute push for legislation to cap the cost of insulin for people with private insurance.

© Alex Brandon / Stephanie Scarbrough, The Associated Press

Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Susan Collins (R-Maine) are both leaving Congress at the end of the year; Shaheen is retiring and Collins lost her re-election bid to Democrat Troy Jackson.

The legislation, which has 28 co-sponsors divided equally between the parties, would cap out-of-pocket costs for insulin at $35 for people with commercial insurance , building off a similar provision for people on Medicare that passed in former President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. It would also create a pilot program in 10 states to cap costs for uninsured people, among other provisions.

The bill cleared the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions in July, putting it closer than ever to final passage.

Lawmakers have discussed the idea of an insulin cap for years but haven’t been able to get legislation over the finish line because of GOP resistance to the government setting prices.

Shaheen argued the midterm election results are a clear sign that voters want lawmakers to pass legislation that makes life more affordable .

“Voters sent a clear message this election that Congress needs to take urgent action to lower costs for American families,” Shaheen said in a statement this week. “With my INSULIN Act, we have a bipartisan opportunity right in front of us to deliver meaningful relief by capping monthly insulin costs at just $35.”

The most likely path forward would be including the measure as part of a year-end spending bill , but it could also be attached to the must-pass defense policy and spending authorization legislation.

A key measure in Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act capped insulin prices to $35 per month for seniors on Medicare. That legislation passed without any GOP support .

Since then, many pharmaceutical companies have voluntarily reduced their prices, but Collins and Shaheen have said it’s not enough .

The cost of insulin has been a barrier to care for many Americans. A monthly cap on patient cost sharing would make the drug cheaper for patients and improve access, but it wouldn’t directly address the underlying price of insulin.

Last week, advocacy organizations, including the National Kidney Foundation and American Diabetes Association, sent letters to the White House and congressional leadership of both parties, urging them to support and immediately pass the legislation .

articles.title: Exclusive: Shaheen, Coons call for ‘swift’ response to Russian incursions into allied airspace
articles.summary: Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.) and Chris Coons (Del.) condemned Russia for its recent reported incursions into the airspace of American allies, saying in a statement shared with The Hill on Friday the U.S. should respond immediately. “This dangerous pattern of hybrid attacks that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin has unleashed on our partners, particularly NATO…
articles.body:
Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.) and Chris Coons (Del.) condemned Russia for its recent reported incursions into the airspace of American allies, saying in a statement shared with The Hill on Friday the U.S. should respond immediately.

“This dangerous pattern of hybrid attacks that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin has unleashed on our partners, particularly NATO countries, is a test of our resolve and an effort to fracture our support for Ukraine,” the senators said.

Multiple U.S. allies reported Russian incursions into their airspace, with Japan and Taiwan both detecting Russian aircraft earlier this week. Poland said Friday multiple Russian “objects,” including a missile, had fallen into the country , and one had exploded. No damage or injuries were reported.

This is not the first time Russian aircraft have entered allied airspace this year; multiple fighter jets from Russia flew over Estonia , a NATO member, in September — a move that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called “unacceptable” at the time.

Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Coons went on to blast President Trump for his friendly posture toward Putin during a trilateral meeting between the pair and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

While in Asia, Trump greeted Xi with an embrace on the tarmac and called Putin his “friend.” At a Friday press briefing, Trump said he had a good relationship with Putin and called it “very good” that Russia has a nuclear weapons stockpile.

“While President Trump gives Vladimir Putin a warm embrace, Russia continues its unacceptable incursions into the airspace of America’s allies,” Shaheen and Coons said.

In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that Trump would meet with any world leader to advocate for U.S. interests.

“President Trump will meet with anyone in order to advance our country’s interests, and his ability to make good deals for the United States has resulted in fair trade agreements, improved nuclear cooperation, expanded market access for American goods, and more,” Kelly said.

Trump’s warm reception of Putin was widely criticized by Democrats and even some Republicans.

“I think his friend invaded a sovereign nation and is responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Thursday. “That’s not company I would keep.”

Trump defended his comments in Friday’s press conference, arguing the U.S. is better off because of his relationship with Xi and Putin.

“You’re very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries,” the president said.

Trump has received backlash from members of both parties for his friendly tone toward Russia in contrast to his sometimes harsh rhetoric about Ukraine and its president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

The president previously said Ukraine should replace Zelensky and blamed high energy costs in the U.S. on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries instead of on the Iran war. Trump struck a deal with Russia this fall to purchase diesel from the country, a move that drew bipartisan backlash.

The president has repeatedly insisted he can bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end. His son-in-law Jared Kushner, who is helping lead negotiations between the two countries, said Thursday that Moscow is open to the idea of Kyiv having a mutual defense pact with Washington.

Russia, however, attacked Ukraine just hours after Trump and Putin’s meeting.

“Putin clearly left these meetings emboldened, not more willing to make peace,” Shaheen and Coons said. “Congress stands firm in our support for America’s allies, and we will maintain our commitment to defend America’s interests and support Ukraine against Russia’s unprovoked aggression.”

articles.title: Trump defends Putin, floats a Stephen Miller presidential run and says he’d work with Dems: News briefing takeaways
articles.summary: President Donald Trump made a high-profile White House briefing room appearance Friday amid a pileup of domestic challenges — including a string of sudden te...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump made a high-profile White House briefing room appearance Friday amid a pileup of domestic challenges — including a string of sudden tech outages, rising artificial intelligence worries and a looming confrontation with Congress' new Democratic majorities.

But before all that, Trump wanted to address a cheerier topic: His continued close personal friendships with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.

"We have a very great relationship," Trump said from the White House after returning from a four-day trip to Asia . "Some of them in this room say, 'Oh, it's terrible he gets along.' I get along with Russia. I get along with China. I get along with a lot of people."

The president spent large swathes of his 90-minute, digression-filled press conference lavishing praise on the two autocrats, despite longstanding concerns within his own administration that the countries are working against the US on key issues.

He hailed the warm reception he received in China, defended his description of Putin as "a friend" and touted a historic trilateral summit that generated little substantive progress on any thorny issues.

Yet as to how he planned to tackle the pressing problems now awaiting him at home, he had few detailed answers at the ready.

Here are six takeaways from Trump's press conference:

Still in a buoyant mood from his multi-day jaunt around the world, Trump on multiple occasions defended his closeness with Putin — even as their regular conversations have brought him no closer to ending Russia's war on Ukraine.

Trump again decried the war's massive casualties and expressed surprise at how difficult it has been to broker peace, chalking the lack of progress to the "tremendous hatred" between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

But he also dismissed the difficult negotiations as partly a "public relations war," while suggesting at one point that Russia's invasion should have "lasted one day" — a remark likely to give Ukraine little assurance of Trump's ongoing support for their defense.

Trump also signaled that his friendship with Putin is rooted in part because they found themselves on the same side during his first-term impeachment over withholding aid to Ukraine.

"I've been dealing with Putin during the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, and to be honest, he was very nice about it," Trump said.

As to whether Putin is as friendly to the US as a whole, the US president was less sure: "I can't speak to America," Trump told CNN's Kaitlan Collins.

Over Trump's right shoulder, Vice President JD Vance . To his left, Secretary of State Marco Rubio . The press conference offered a striking visual of the shadow primary likely to play out over the next several months, as possible 2028 presidential contenders led by Vance and Rubio weigh their options and jockey for Trump's favor.

And Trump leaned in to the show of it all — inviting both men to talk before orchestrating a twist ending.

Rubio, who traveled to Asia with Trump, delivered an extended account of the trip and its takeaways, focusing in particular on the benefits that it could deliver to the US economy and its national security. He also mounted a more polished defense of Trump's meeting with Putin and Xi than Trump did himself.

"The better these three leaders get along, the easier and more conducive the environment will be to actually agree to things that are concrete down the road," Rubio argued.

As for Vance — who stayed behind as others went to Asia, as is customary for vice presidents — he sought to make light of the dynamics that were sure to be dissected by close 2028 watchers.

"I would liken it a little bit to Home Alone, but with better food and more gold," he joked. So, I miss you, sir."

Vance went on to highlight the passage of a bipartisan permitting reform bill. And he got a boost from Trump, who denied reports that he was upset with Vance for blaming the GOP's midterm losses on the Iran war. (In Trump's telling, he only wished Vance would have said the war was still worth it, which Vance pointedly did not do.)

But neither Vance nor Rubio were the true stars of the day in Trump's eyes. That was his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.

"The most powerful man in the room right now," Trump said of Miller, who, at least until now, has not signaled 2028 ambitions. "He was better than these two guys. Do you want to run for president?"

Trump did have one new policy announcement to make: A planned crackdown on US companies building data centers outside the country.

The president vowed to hit US companies with a "tremendous tax" if they try to build data centers elsewhere, arguing that there is plenty of domestic demand for the structures powering the AI boom.

But it's unclear what tax penalties companies would face if they don't comply, and Trump conceded he hadn't even briefed his team on the idea yet. It also appeared out of step with public opinion. Polls show Americans are overwhelmingly more concerned about data center construction than excited by it. Trump, though, was not one of those Americans.

"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," he said.

Trump openly acknowledged during the press conference that the Iran war had soured Americans' mood and cost his party politically. But he showed no signs of backing off a fight that he repeatedly insisted was necessary to prevent the Iranian regime from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

"Watch my lips," Trump said at one point. "Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, ever."

He went on to deem Iran's leaders "crazy" and insisted he had no regrets about how he's prosecuted the war, even as he appeared to acknowledge that some in his administration feel differently.

"People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion," he said. "But I say, I know the Iranians. And frankly, they're crazy."

Still, Trump had far less to say on the more pressing question: How he plans to definitively win the war and extract the US from the Middle East. The White House has yet to articulate that strategy, and on Friday, all Trump could offer was that Iran was "bullsh*tting" him, and he was surprised that the economic damage from the conflict hadn't been worse.

"The war drove up prices, fuel prices, far less than I thought," he said. "I thought it would go up to $300 a barrel."

An offer to Dems: Olive branch or veto pen

Pressed on how he planned to spend his final two years in office opposite a Democratic Congress, Trump laid out two futures for himself: As a bipartisan dealmaker, or a hardline issuer of vetoes. The choice would be up to Democrats, he insisted.

"They could go two years and one month, because that's what we have, and I'm going to veto them," Trump said. But "if they want to get things done, I want to get things done."

He added that the next two years working with Democrats could be even more productive than before, lamenting the constant opposition he faced from a handful of Republicans, including Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky. Trump even had two possible deals in mind already: A federal film credit meant to strengthen Hollywood and college sports legislation setting national standards for how athletes can profit from their name, likeness and image.

Trump floated deals on bigger topics, as well: Health care and immigration.

But he gave few details on what those deals might entail, and whether there might be any true common ground between Democrats and Republicans on the two issues they've already spent decades fighting over.

Another sign that Trump may end up taking the veto path: His empowerment of Miller, an immigration hardliner who has overseen the administration's deportation campaign.

"They think he's hard on immigration," Trump said. "He's got a tremendous heart."

The growing bipartisan push for tighter restrictions on advanced chip sales for China hasn't dimmed Trump's admiration for the two men at the center of the controversy: Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick .

Trump endorsed reinstalling Huang atop Nvidia despite his reported extramarital affairs, including one suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. And he voiced support for Lutnick, even as he comes under fire from Republicans for resisting efforts meant to prevent chips from begin diverted to China.

"I'd like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back," Trump said. "I would love to see him be back."

As for Lutnick: "I have not lost confidence."

Nvidia has made clear it has no plans to reinstate Huang . And by keeping Lutnick atop Commerce, even Trump acknowledged that it could create complications for the administration, as Democrats and even some Republicans in Congress launch investigations into his conduct. But he still believes in Lutnick, he maintained.

"He has a natural business instinct," Trump said. "I think he's doing a very good job."

articles.title: Trump says US flight systems are 'ancient' but 'safe' after ground stop
articles.summary: Trump backed members of his administration who are asking for $50bn to rebuild air traffic control systems in the wake of last Friday's major outage.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said air traffic control systems that manage flights across the country are "ancient" and is pushing Congress to fund costly upgrades.

Trump called the systems "obsolete", saying they were at least "55 years old" and noted some towers were not in good shape structurally.

"It's very safe. But it's safe for a different reason because we do it very slowly," he said. "In other words, we travel slower. That's why you have lots of waits at the airport."

His remarks came a week after a historic ground stop halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the agency planned on Friday to share more information about what led to the four-hour ground stop on 13 November.

Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.

At a press briefing, Trump responded to some concerns about whether the ground stop issue was at all linked to other tech outages in the same week.

"They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has explained a government contractor was upgrading an aviation telecommunications network, swapping out copper lines for fibre and installing a router, which directs traffic across the network.

The switch led the router to start flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. It is unclear whether the root cause of the issue was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced issues with voice and ground communications. It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.

More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled the day of the outage, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5mn passengers.

Ripple effects from the incident caused issues for days, with thousands more flights being cancelled or delayed over the weekend.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or return to gates.

The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.

How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos

Since the outage, transportation leaders have repeatedly pressed Congress for billions in funding to upgrade US systems and warned that without an overhaul outages like this would continue.

Trump on Friday weighed in and backed members of his administration, who are asking for $50bn (£38bn) to rebuild air traffic control systems. He said the transportation department had been allotted $12bn (£9bn), which is not enough for such a large undertaking.

"I said, 'Sean, let's not spend money to patch up all over the place because when we get the new system, everything's going to be torn out, so let's not spend the 12. Spend as little as you can to keep it going,'" Trump said he told Duffy, the transportation secretary.

He reiterated accusations that Congress - which is currently controlled by the Republican party - was blocking the funds.

"We need to have new air traffic control, and to do that we have to get the money now," Trump said.

"Congress has been very bad on it, but if there's any silver lining to what happened last week, it's that Congress seems to be very receptive now to giving us the money."

articles.title: Fiona the hippo honored by US Senate in unanimous resolution praising Cincinnati Zoo staff
articles.summary: Fiona the hippo received a formal Senate tribute from Sen. Bernie Moreno one day after the Cincinnati Zoo Nile hippopotamus died after a medical emergency.
articles.body: Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent. Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident. BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT "The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno said. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart." The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was launched over the viewing windows into her habitat. "The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the zoo said in a Thursday statement. "Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome." 'WORST AQUARIUM EVER' REVIEW SENDS WHALING MUSEUM'S SALES SOARING 250% Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, rose to international fame in January 2017 after she was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds. Her survival drew millions of followers online and inspired books, clothing, beer and an ice cream flavor. Tributes poured in across Ohio and Capitol Hill following her death, with Sen. articles.title: Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa vows to rescind Abbott's H-1B visa restrictions despite admitting program abuse
articles.summary: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa says she will rescind Greg Abbott's H-1B hiring freeze on day one, even conceding companies have abused the visa program.
articles.body: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) said she plans to rescind Gov. Greg Abbott’s hiring freeze on H-1B visa workers at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even as she acknowledged that the federal visa program has been abused. In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction. "Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa said. Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing new H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY "In the most egregious schemes, employers have even fired American workers and replaced them with H-1B employees, often at lower wages," Abbott wrote in his January directive. While Hinojosa vowed to scrap the restrictions, she conceded that companies have exploited the visa system. "There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune. "Companies should not be getting a bunch of tax breaks for jobs to only then use that money to hire H-1B employees. That’s wrong. That’s happening right now. I don’t support that." Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative from Austin, defeated Abbott in the Nov. 3 election to deny the three-term Republican incumbent a fourth term, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. With Republicans still holding a majority in the Texas Senate, rescinding Abbott’s executive orders offers Hinojosa an immediate way to reshape state policy without legislative approval. HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT FUELS 11TH-HOUR POWER STRUGGLE AS NEW ALLIES RALLY TO REIN IN INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR Hinojosa also defended local school districts’ use of H-1B visas to recruit foreign educators, arguing that Texas schools struggle to find domestic teachers. Abbott’s directive, however, applies only to state agencies and public institutions of higher education, not local K-12 school districts. A representative for Hinojosa did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. articles.title: Fachin tenta acelerar reformas no STF sob resistência interna | G1
articles.standfirst: Condução no caso Master ainda gera desgastes internos para o presidente do STF. Fachin quer agilizar respostas e facilitar o acesso à Justiça.
articles.summary: Fachin busca consenso para um novo código de ética e mudanças no sistema de Justiça enquanto lida com desgastes do caso Banco Master e críticas a penduricalhos.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), ministro Edson Fachin , tenta avançar, a um mês do início do recesso, com pautas internas que dividem a Suprema Corte. O STF entra em recesso formalmente no dia 20 de dezembro.

São três questões centrais da agenda de Fachin que ainda enfrentam resistência e podem se estenderam para 2027:

código de ética para ministros dos Tribunais Superiores; e

relatórios da PF sobre menções a ministros e parentes no caso Master.

Fachin criou um grupo para discutir melhorias e modernização do sistema de Justiça em meio a críticas pelos pagamentos milionários dos chamados penduricalhos, que acabaram limitados pelo STF.

Além disso, o Judiciário é cobrado por maior transparência e rigor ético por parte da magistratura, inclusive de ministros do STF, que acabou arrastado para a crise do Banco Master.

O objetivo de Fachin é agilizar respostas e facilitar o acesso à Justiça. A ideia do presidente do STF é que o grupo feche um relatório até 10 de dezembro e a versão final no dia 19 de dezembro.

São esperadas sugestões de mudança legislativas, que dependem do Congresso Nacional para se concretizar, mas também questões administrativas, como modificações no regimento do STF e do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ).

Integrantes do grupo afirmam de forma reservada que há risco de não conseguir concluir todas as análises até o início do recesso e que ainda há muitas ideias sem convergência e que ainda não foram apresentadas propostas para discussão.

O grupo recebeu contribuições de 87 instituições, com centenas de propostas que trazem pontos polêmicos como:

adoção de mandato para ministros do STF;

A interlocutores, o presidente do STF tem indicado que vai insistir no cronograma inicial.

Presidente do Supremo Tribunal Fedreal (STF), ministro Edson Fachin — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

Em outra frente, Fachin vem conversando com a ministra Cármen Lúcia sobre a elaboração de um código de ética para ministros da Corte.

O presidente do tribunal já apresentou sugestões para a relatora, que deve elaborar uma minuta. A proposta deve tentar contemplar ideias que sejam consensos.

A indicação é de que o texto será enviado a Fachin até o fim de novembro. O anteprojeto elaborado pela relatora terá que ser aprovado pelos ministros.

Um dos pontos que deve ser enfrentado é a divulgação de participação de ministros em palestras, tema que enfrenta resistências no STF.

Uma das discussões é quanto à necessidade de divulgação prévia e se isso pode representar algum risco à segurança dos ministros.

Outra controvérsia seria a instituir fiscalização do descumprimento das regras de um código de ética e a quem caberia o papel de fiscalizador.

Fachin ainda tenta contornar a crise que se instalou no STF por conta do escândalo do Master. Internamente, o presidente é criticado pela condução da crise, mas vem sinalizando a interlocutores que vai continuar fazendo o que acha correto.

Fachin enviou para a Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) o material reunido pela Polícia Federal a partir do celular de Vorcaro.

Só depois de manifestação da Procuradoria é que Fachin deve levar eventuais caso para análise do plenário do Supremo. Não há um prazo para isso. Uma ala da Corte avalia que isso só deve ocorrer em 2027.

articles.title: Sotomayor suggests Supreme Court colleagues may applaud midterm results as safeguard
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor on Friday suggested her colleagues may view Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections as a sign that their recent immunity decision has not eliminated checks on the president. Speaking in Philadelphia, the liberal justice replied “absolutely” when asked if her colleagues were counting on elections as an institutional safeguard…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor on Friday suggested her colleagues may view Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections as a sign that their recent immunity decision has not eliminated checks on the president.

Speaking in Philadelphia, the liberal justice replied “absolutely” when asked if her colleagues were counting on elections as an institutional safeguard when issuing their landmark ruling granting Trump and former presidents broad criminal immunity.

“My colleagues today would probably applaud the last election, because they believe that if the people don’t like what’s happening, they can speak with their vote. And they did speak,” Sotomayor said.

“Now, they may not have liked the message — but I don’t know that,” she continued, “but what I do know is that they really did believe that, structurally, those things are what protect us against excesses in executive power.”

Sotomayor has continued to publicly rail against the 6-3 decision that granted Trump and former presidents presumptive criminal immunity for their official acts, recently saying she hopes the decision will ultimately be overturned.

On Friday, speaking at an American Philosophical Society event, Sotomayor again condemned the decision and said she doesn’t believe the remaining institutional controls in the political system are enough.

“I think what they missed was the concept that there was no man in this country — and I use the male version, because that’s the saying — that no man was above the law here,” she said of her colleagues. “I think [that] was always something that was an important part of the calculus in which executives made their decision.” Sotomayor notably didn’t shut down talk of Supreme Court term limits when asked by an audience member during the 45-minute discussion, though she said it was up to elected officials to decide. The justice noted other countries that don’t have judicial lifetime appointments.

“They either have age limits or they have term limits,” Sotomayor said. “So, they have not needed it to keep um politics out of influencing their judges in the way our founders worried. So, that’s something that should give you pause.”

articles.title: Permitting reform bill clears major hurdle toward becoming law
articles.summary: Presented by EQT {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Senate approves major permitting reform bill The Senate passed a major bill Thursday seeking to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy production and infrastructure — taking a massive step toward the legislation becoming law. Greg Nash The bill was passed…
articles.body:
Senate approves major permitting reform bill

The Senate passed a major bill Thursday seeking to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy production and infrastructure — taking a massive step toward the legislation becoming law.

The bill was passed by a vote of 62-33, with most of the Senate GOP’s support. Just two Republicans , Sens. Mike Rounds (S.D.) and Josh Hawley (Mo.), voted against the legislation.

While it was a bipartisan effort — spearheaded by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) — Democratic support in the upper chamber was more limited .

The bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), seeks to address long-standing complaints from various industries that infrastructure projects take too long to build in the U.S.

The legislation now heads to the House , where it’s also expected to have significant bipartisan support despite a split among Democrats. The White House is backing the bill, and it has issued a statement of support saying BAAJA “would remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.”

In the House, the Democratic caucus is divided on the bill. It appears to have significant GOP support — although at least one powerful Republican said he’d like to see some changes to the legislation.

The bill also contends with a crowded lame-duck calendar and absences . On Friday, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) called on his colleagues to show up and vote on issues including permitting reform.

“We’re getting very positive signals,” Capito told reporters when asked about the bill’s prospects in the House. She also noted supporters had spoken with several groups in the lower chamber but cautioned, “I would take nothing for granted.”

The bill aims to improve the nation’s ability to build power lines — a key step in getting renewable energy projects onto the grid — by allowing federal regulators to approve their construction if states don’t act.

It contains provisions that seek to prevent presidents from yanking existing permits from energy of all types — combating President Trump’s ability to block already approved wind projects and moves made by Democratic presidents, such as revoking approval from the Keystone XL pipeline.

BAAJA also exempts certain activities , including expansions to natural gas pipelines, from environmental reviews and limits those reviews to only alternatives that meet the goal of a project’s sponsor company.

It additionally restricts lawsuits against projects by mandating they be filed within 150 days of a proposal’s approval.

The bill also seeks to rein in increased electricity costs from large data centers, forcing them to pay for any costs stemming from their high electricity demand.

articles.title: California man found guilty of sparking blaze that became deadly Palisades Fire
articles.summary: The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) – A federal jury on Friday convicted a former Uber driver on arson charges for deliberately starting a brush fire that smoldered before eventually exploding into the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

Jurors in Los Angeles deliberated for about two and a half hours before reaching a verdict.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht used a lighter to ignite the Lachman Fire in the Santa Monica Mountains near Pacific Palisades on Jan. 1, 2025. After fire crews responded and believed they had extinguished the fire, it continued to burn underground for days and reignited as the deadly Palisades Fire.

The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht was arrested in Florida nine months later.

Prosecutors argued the former Uber driver was frustrated with his place in society and harbored anger toward wealthy people.

Shortly after midnight on New Year’s Eve, after dropping off a passenger in Pacific Palisades, prosecutors said he walked up a trail, took videos from a nearby hilltop area and listened to music, with the video showing objects being lit on fire.

The conviction comes after a jury was unable to reach a verdict in Rinderknecht’s first trial in June. In that trial, the jury deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal.

Prosecutors also dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.

During the second trial, prosecutors focused on evidence placing Rinderknecht at the fire’s origin and established that he was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times after the Lachman Fire began as he walked down the hill, according to evidence presented at the trial.

Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

The Palisades Fire began in the Santa Monica Mountains of Los Angeles County on Jan. 7, 2025, and grew to destroy large areas of Pacific Palisades, Topanga, and Malibu before it was fully contained on Jan. 31. Twelve people were killed and 6,837 structures were destroyed.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
